title: Most systems with non-simple behavior are computationally irreducible

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Most systems with non-simple behavior are computationally irreducible

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Predicting a system's outcome by a mathematical shortcut is normally possible only for special systems with simple behavior; other systems are computationally irreducible, so their behavior can be found only by tracing each step with roughly as much computational effort as the system itself expends.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 1: The Foundations for a New Kind of Science

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: such systems are computationally irreducible—so that in effect the only way to find their behavior is to trace each of their steps, spending about as much computational effort as the systems themselves.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 1, “The Foundations for a New Kind of Science”; section “An Outline of Basic Ideas” (from p. 1), p. 6. Scope: systems whose behavior is not obviously simple

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch01-08: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.41

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Irreducibility can be proved for carefully formalized systems and tasks, so restricted cases are resolvable. Existing theory and computation cannot establish the broad prevalence claim over vaguely defined non-simple systems.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Define prediction tasks, computational cost, and a distribution over systems, then prove lower bounds or benchmark all known shortcut algorithms against direct simulation. Lower bounds matching simulation would confirm irreducibility for specified systems; a broadly faster predictor would refute it there.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Special prediction questions may be easy even when full trajectories are hard.

Normally and roughly as much effort require an unspecified measure and distribution.

General computational lower bounds are exceptionally difficult.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Bounded prediction experiments on elementary cellular automata and other small systems are routine and can show that many non-simple rules lack obvious shortcuts. That is a proxy for a bounded horizon, not a proof that most systems are irreducible in the strong sense. Undecidability blocks a general algorithm that would certify the majority claim across its stated scope.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: On a declared ensemble of non-simple systems, search for predictors whose cost grows slower than direct simulation, including closed forms, periodicity, and statistical shortcuts. A system is treated as irreducible on a finite horizon if every such predictor fails. The majority claim is confirmed only if that failure holds for most of the ensemble, which a finite search cannot fully prove.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The ensemble of 'most systems' is open-ended, so small rule spaces are a subset.

Failure to find a shortcut does not prove that none exists.

Irreducibility of arbitrary systems is entangled with undecidability.
